name: Malathi
definition: Malathi is a composite portrait of a woman working in the pepper and spice trade in the Malnad belt of Shivamogga district, drawing on the occupational patterns of families who moved from traditional areca cultivation into processing work. She represents households navigating the tension between agricultural heritage and wage labour, forest-fringe life and human-wildlife conflict, and the aspiration to give children urban-oriented schooling despite the geographic and economic constraints of Ghat-taluk residence.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Malathi works six-hour shifts five or six days a week at a small pepper-curing and sorting unit on the Hosanagara-Sagara road, grading dried pepper, packing spice orders and occasionally helping with cardamom when the season demands it. The unit is owned by a trader who buys from estates across Hosanagara and Tirthahalli taluks and sells to wholesalers in Mangaluru and Bengaluru. She earns around nine thousand rupees a month, paid weekly in cash, with no formal contract or provident fund. The work is indoors and less physically demanding than field labour, which matters because her knees have troubled her since a fall three years ago. Her husband, Ramesh, owns a small three-acre areca and coconut plot inherited from his father, but prices have been poor for two years and Yellow Leaf Disease has weakened several palms. He also drives an auto-rickshaw on the Hosanagara town route two or three days a week to cover household shortfalls. The combined family income hovers around twenty thousand rupees a month in good months, less when areca prices drop or pepper-unit orders slow. Expenses are high: school fees, provisions bought from the town ration shop and private vendors, medical costs and loan repayments to a local self-help group and a private moneylender. Fuel, fertiliser and pesticide for the areca plot drain whatever the land yields. Malathi starts her day at five-thirty, cooks breakfast and lunch, walks twenty minutes to catch a share-auto to the unit, works until two or three in the afternoon, returns home to cook dinner and helps her older daughter with homework. Weekends are for weeding the areca plot, washing clothes and attending the village temple. The rhythm is tight, money is always calculated to the week, and there is no savings cushion for an emergency.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Malathi lives with her husband Ramesh, their two daughters—fourteen-year-old Shruti and eleven-year-old Priya—and Ramesh's widowed mother, Sharada, who is sixty-eight and manages the household when Malathi is at work. Sharada cooks the midday meal, feeds the two chickens and one cow they keep, and watches the younger girl when school closes early. Malathi's own parents live in a village near Sringeri in Chikkamagaluru district; she visits them once or twice a year, usually during a festival or when someone is ill. Her marriage was arranged when she was nineteen, following Havyaka Brahmin custom, and she moved to Hosanagara taluk after the wedding. Ramesh is forty-one and comes from a family that once had a larger areca holding, but it was divided among three brothers twenty years ago. His two brothers have both left for Bengaluru—one works in a hardware shop, the other as a clerk—and rarely return except for major occasions. Gender roles are traditional: Malathi does all the cooking, cleaning and childcare, while Ramesh handles field work, auto-driving and interactions with traders and officials. Sharada expects both girls to marry into Havyaka families, though Malathi quietly hopes Shruti will finish a degree first. Decisions about spending, schooling and medical treatment are made by Ramesh after consultation with Malathi and his mother, but major choices—like whether to sell a portion of the land—rest with the men.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Malathi studied up to seventh standard at the government school in her natal village before her parents pulled her out to help at home and prepare for marriage; girls' secondary schooling was less common in Havyaka families in the 1990s, though that is slowly changing. Shruti, the elder daughter, is in ninth standard at the government high school in Hosanagara town, a forty-minute journey by bus each way. The school is better-equipped than the taluk's village schools, with a science lab and English-medium sections, but Shruti travels in a crowded KSRTC bus that is often late, and during the monsoon months from June to September the Sharavathi tributary near their village swells and the road becomes difficult. Priya, the younger daughter, is in sixth standard at the same school. The family pays around fifteen hundred rupees per term for books, uniforms and miscellaneous fees, plus the cost of daily bus fares under the Shakti scheme is now free for the girls, which has been a relief. Sharada grumbles that girls do not need so much education, but Malathi insists that Shruti should at least finish tenth standard and sit the SSLC exam; she dreams of Shruti becoming a teacher or a government clerk, something with a steady salary and respect. Ramesh agrees in principle but worries about the cost of PU college if Shruti passes tenth, and whether they can afford to send her to Hassan or Shivamogga town for further study. Priya is a weaker student and sometimes skips school claiming stomach aches; Malathi suspects she is anxious about English and mathematics, subjects the village primary school barely taught. The household's schooling hope is that one daughter will secure a government job and lift the family, but the fear is that Shruti will have to stop after tenth if money runs out or if a good marriage proposal comes early.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Malathi's knee pain, the result of a slip on wet mud three years ago, flares up during the monsoon and when she stands for long hours at the curing unit; she takes ibuprofen tablets bought from the Hosanagara town pharmacy and sometimes uses a turmeric-oil rub Sharada prepares. She has never seen an orthopaedic specialist; the nearest is in Shivamogga town, a two-hour journey, and the consultation and scans would cost thousands they do not have. Ramesh suffers from seasonal respiratory trouble, probably from pesticide exposure on the areca plot and auto-rickshaw exhaust; he uses an inhaler during bad months. Sharada has high blood pressure and diabetes, managed with tablets from the government taluk hospital, and she attends a monthly check-up though the wait is often three or four hours. The family uses the taluk hospital for fevers, minor injuries and antenatal check-ups, and the anganwadi nurse for the girls' immunisations when they were younger. For serious illness—like when Priya had dengue two years ago—they went to a private clinic in Hosanagara and borrowed five thousand rupees to cover the drips and tests. Malathi worries about Kyasanur Forest Disease because monkeys are common around the areca plot and several neighbours have fallen ill during the January-to-May peak season; the vaccination drive reached their village last year but Sharada refused the injection, calling it dangerous, and Malathi could not convince her. Snakebites and leopard scares are also real: a neighbour's cow was killed by a leopard last year and a boy from the next village died of a snakebite before he could reach hospital. Malathi ties a red thread and a black bead on Priya's schoolbag for protection, a habit Sharada insists on. Mental health is not named, but Malathi feels a constant low-level anxiety—about money, about Shruti's future, about the rains and the forest—and she prays at the village Sharadamba shrine every Thursday for peace of mind.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Malathi's family belongs to the Havyaka Brahmin community, traditionally areca cultivators and priests concentrated in the Malnad belt across Shivamogga, Chikkamagaluru and parts of Uttara Kannada. Havyaka families speak a distinct dialect of Kannada and maintain vegetarian households; Malathi's family observes all traditional rituals and festivals, with Sharada leading daily prayers to a small shrine of Sharadamba and Ganapati in the house. The family visits the Sringeri Sharada Peetham once or twice a year, a pilgrimage Sharada insists on, and Malathi feels a deep reverence for the temple and the Jagadguru. Within Hosanagara taluk the Havyaka community is a small minority; most neighbours are Vokkaliga, Kuruba, Gowda and Scheduled Caste families, and relations are polite but not close. Malathi's workplace at the pepper unit includes women from various communities and castes, and they share tea and talk during breaks, but socialising beyond work is rare. Sharada is stricter about caste rules than Malathi, refusing to eat food cooked by non-Brahmins and insisting the girls marry within the Havyaka fold. Malathi is more pragmatic, though she has not openly challenged her mother-in-law's views. The family does not participate in village panchayat politics, leaving that to Vokkaliga and Gowda households who dominate local leadership. Malathi's sense of community is layered: Havyaka Brahmin identity, Kannada-speaking Malnad identity and a vague notion of being from a "cultured" priestly lineage, all of which sit uneasily with the reality of wage labour and declining areca income. She takes pride in Kuvempu, the Jnanpith poet from nearby Kuppalli, whose house-museum she visited once on a school trip decades ago, and she tells Shruti that educated families like theirs must preserve Kannada and culture even when times are hard.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Malathi's household has a yellow ration card, which provides subsidised rice, wheat and kerosene, though the quantities have been less generous in recent years and the fair-price shop sometimes runs out of stock. Ramesh applied for a Kisan Credit Card but was refused because his three-acre holding is considered too small and informally split with his brothers, so he borrows from a self-help group linked to SKDRDP and from a private moneylender at higher interest. Malathi is a member of a women's self-help group that meets monthly in the village; she has taken two small loans over the years, one for Shruti's school fees and one to repair the roof after a storm. The group also organised a government training on organic farming last year, which Ramesh attended, though he has not adopted any of the methods. The family's main interaction with government is through the taluk hospital, the girls' school and the electricity board, whose power cuts during the monsoon can last hours. Ramesh once applied for compensation after a fallen tree blocked the road to their areca plot for two weeks, but the application was lost in the tahsildar's office and he gave up. She knows B.S. Yediyurappa's name because he is from Shivamogga and was chief minister, but she cannot name the current MLA. The 2018 state election and the 2019 national election brought campaign jeeps and promises of loan waivers, none of which materialised. The Kasturirangan Western Ghats notification has been a topic of worry since 2026: Ramesh attended a public meeting in Hosanagara where farmer leaders said the notification would prevent areca replanting and infrastructure, and he came home angry, calling it another way the government punishes Malnad while favouring Bengaluru. Malathi trusts little from government except the ration shop and the anganwadi nurse, and she believes getting ahead requires either a government job, which is nearly impossible without connections, or leaving the village entirely.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Malathi worries most about Shruti's future: whether the girl will pass her SSLC, whether they can afford to send her to PU college, and whether she will find a good husband who does not demand a large dowry. She fears that if Shruti stops schooling after tenth, she will end up like Malathi herself—married young, working for small wages, dependent on a husband's uncertain income. She is proud that Shruti is bright and disciplined, and she tells herself that education is the only ladder out of this life, but she also knows that money may force a different choice. Malathi worries about the areca plot: whether Yellow Leaf Disease will spread further, whether the rains will be good, whether Ramesh will be forced to sell the land to pay off the moneylender. She blames the government for not controlling areca prices and for ignoring Malnad farmers while spending crores on Bengaluru metro and IT parks. She blames the Forest Department for restricting access to minor forest produce and for failing to compensate quickly when elephants or leopards destroy crops or livestock; a neighbour waited two years for compensation after an elephant raid, and the amount was a fraction of the loss. She is ashamed that she works in a curing unit for daily wages, a job she thinks is beneath a Brahmin woman, but she does not voice this shame except in prayers. She demands that the government keep schools open during the monsoon, build a bridge over the river near the village so children do not miss classes, and guarantee areca prices through a minimum-support scheme like paddy. She wishes Malnad were not forgotten, that roads were better, that hospitals were closer, and that her daughters could study without fear of having to stop. She prays to Sharadamba every day for the strength to hold the household together and for Shruti to pass tenth standard with good marks.
